strengths: Clear and practically relevant idea: pretrain a neural posterior estimator on inexpensive low-fidelity simulations and fine-tune it with limited high-fidelity data.
Evaluation covers a tractable benchmark and two computationally demanding neuroscience simulators, including a challenging 24-parameter spiking-network model.

The paper reports several diagnostics, including C2ST, negative log probability of true parameters, posterior predictive checks, and limited simulation-based calibration, with repeated network initializations.
The presentation is generally clear, with algorithms, prior specifications, simulator descriptions, and candid discussion of some limitations.
weaknesses: The baseline suite is inadequate. Most comparisons are only against standard NPE; critically, MF-TSNPE is not compared with randomly initialized TSNPE, so the benefit of multifidelity pretraining cannot be separated from that of sequential inference. Comparisons with cited multifidelity likelihood-free methods and stronger transfer or joint-training controls are also absent.

Computational-efficiency claims are not supported by total-cost comparisons. Plots count only high-fidelity simulations and exclude low-fidelity simulation and training costs. In the neuron experiment, low fidelity is only about seven times cheaper, so 10^4 low-fidelity simulations cost roughly 1.4×10^3 high-fidelity-equivalent simulations and may eliminate the advertised savings.

The technical contribution is essentially weight initialization followed by ordinary fine-tuning. There is no theory, principled measure of fidelity relatedness, or systematic study of negative transfer. All low-fidelity models are favorable, hand-designed choices, leaving unclear when the method helps or fails.

The acquisition variant intentionally changes the proposal without correction and can therefore produce biased posterior estimates. Limiting acquired samples to 20% is only a heuristic, and the paper provides neither a correctness argument nor sufficient calibration evidence for this variant; its empirical improvement is also minor relative to its extra cost.

Evidence on the scientific tasks is incomplete. Evaluations use synthetic simulator-generated observations rather than real data, NLTP does not by itself establish posterior accuracy, and calibration evidence is sparse. The 24-parameter experiment relies mainly on NLTP and a broad firing-rate validity criterion.

Important reproducibility details are missing or unclear, including optimizer settings, learning rate, batch size, exact early-stopping rule, per-round allocation, acquisition-pool size, and end-to-end cost. The sequential algorithm also appears to train only on the current round rather than accumulated data and needs clarification.

Claims of one-to-two-order computational savings and “real-world” applications are stronger than the presented evidence. Given the limited novelty, missing decisive baselines, and lack of cost-normalized evaluation, the paper is not yet competitive for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: reducing the number of expensive simulations required for neural posterior estimation.
MF-NPE is simple, clearly presented, and potentially useful when a genuinely informative low-fidelity simulator is readily available.

The experiments include an analytically tractable benchmark and two scientifically relevant neuroscience simulators, with multiple high-fidelity budgets and some posterior predictive and calibration analyses.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited: the main method is standard low-fidelity pretraining followed by high-fidelity fine-tuning, without theoretical analysis or a principled characterization of when transfer should help or fail.

The baseline set is inadequate. Comparisons are largely restricted to plain NPE; the paper omits standalone TSNPE for the sequential experiments, existing multifidelity likelihood-free methods, joint LF/HF training, and controls such as pretraining on the prior or an unrelated simulator. Consequently, gains cannot be cleanly attributed to informative multifidelity transfer.

The central efficiency claim is not supported by total-cost accounting. Results are plotted only against the number of high-fidelity simulations, ignoring low-fidelity simulation and training costs. In the neuron task, 100,000 low-fidelity simulations with only a sevenfold cost advantage correspond to roughly 14,000 high-fidelity-equivalent simulations, which can eliminate the claimed savings. No end-to-end runtime or compute comparison is reported.

Evidence of posterior accuracy is weak on the two neuroscience tasks. NLTP alone is insufficient, the posterior-predictive and SBC checks are limited, and the 24-parameter spiking-network problem is evaluated using only two summary statistics. The reported fraction of samples producing plausible firing rates does not establish posterior correctness.

The experiments use simulator-generated observations rather than real empirical data, so describing the neuroscience evaluations as real-world tasks and referring to matched empirical data overstates the evidence.

The acquisition variant deliberately mixes actively selected samples into training without proposal correction, introducing acknowledged posterior bias. Its improvement is minor, yet bias and calibration are not rigorously investigated.

Uncertainty estimates largely vary network initialization while holding the simulation dataset fixed, so they do not measure variability arising from the finite simulation budget. This is particularly problematic in the claimed low-budget regime.

Reproducibility is insufficient and internally inconsistent: the neuron stimulus is described as noisy 0.3 nA in the main text but as 0.55 mV without the same noise specification in the appendix; the high-dimensional example is described once as having 14 parameters but elsewhere as 24; optimizer, learning rate, batch size, early-stopping details, and seeds are absent; and a codebase is mentioned without a provided link.

There is no systematic study of negative transfer or low-/high-fidelity mismatch. The assertion that domain experts will know whether a low-fidelity model is adequate does not replace diagnostics or robustness experiments, and substantially narrows the demonstrated applicability.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck in simulation-based inference: learning posteriors when high-fidelity simulations are expensive. The proposed transfer-learning formulation is simple, broadly applicable, and easy to integrate with NPE and TSNPE.

The evaluation covers complementary settings: an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck task with an analytical reference posterior, a multicompartment neuron model, and a challenging 24-parameter spiking-network application. This is substantially more convincing than evaluation on toy benchmarks alone.

MF-NPE consistently improves over training NPE from scratch, particularly at small high-fidelity simulation budgets. The paper also reports C2ST, negative log-probability of true parameters, posterior predictive checks, simulation-based calibration, confidence intervals, and results over multiple observations and network initializations.

The experiments use scientifically meaningful low-fidelity models rather than arbitrary corruptions. The mean-field approximation for the spiking-network application is an especially compelling demonstration of how domain knowledge can reduce reliance on expensive simulation.
The manuscript is clear and well organized, discusses limitations, and provides useful implementation and simulator details in the appendix.
weaknesses: The baseline evaluation is too narrow. Most experiments compare only against standard NPE, while the sequential variants are evaluated only on the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck task. Comparisons with multifidelity ABC approaches where feasible, alternative transfer or joint-training strategies, and stronger sequential SBI baselines would better establish the contribution.

The efficiency claims count high-fidelity simulations rather than total computational cost. This can be misleading when many low-fidelity simulations are used: for the neuron task, the low-fidelity simulator is only approximately seven times cheaper, so pretraining on 100,000 low-fidelity samples may cost more than the high-fidelity simulations ostensibly saved. End-to-end simulator and training time comparisons are needed to substantiate the claimed reductions.

The empirical study does not systematically characterize negative transfer or sensitivity to the mismatch between fidelities. Varying the fidelity gap, including deliberately weak low-fidelity models, or comparing against unrelated pretraining would clarify when MF-NPE helps or hurts.

The proposed acquisition-function extension yields only minor gains, introduces extra computation and hyperparameters, and deliberately omits a proposal correction. Consequently, A-MF-TSNPE may produce biased posterior estimates, and the current experiments do not sufficiently quantify that bias.

Several reproducibility and statistical details remain incomplete, including the precise early-stopping rule, optimizer and training schedule, acquisition-pool size, and full end-to-end resource requirements. Reported uncertainty also appears to emphasize network initialization while using fixed simulation datasets, leaving variability across training datasets insufficiently assessed.

The main mechanism is weight initialization through low-fidelity pretraining, which is technically straightforward. The paper's significance therefore depends heavily on empirical validation; the limited baseline set and lack of compute-normalized comparisons prevent a stronger accept score.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck in simulation-based inference: reducing the use of computationally expensive high-fidelity simulators.
The core MF-NPE idea is simple, technically plausible, and broadly applicable: pretrain a neural posterior estimator on low-fidelity simulations and fine-tune it on high-fidelity data.

The evaluation spans several controlled benchmarks, high-dimensional image observations, and two substantive neuroscience simulators, with results generally showing strong gains in high-fidelity simulation efficiency at small budgets.
The paper includes useful analyses of low-/high-fidelity mismatch, parameter-space mismatch, posterior calibration, posterior predictive checks, and end-to-end computational cost.
The presentation is clear and the appendices provide substantial architectural, simulator, prior, and algorithmic detail.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited: the main method is essentially standard transfer learning applied to neural posterior estimation. The paper provides no theory specific to multifidelity transfer; the stated convergence proof is only the standard population-risk argument for ordinary NPE.

The experimental comparison is too narrow for a top-tier contribution. The principal baselines are NPE and TSNPE, while the MF-ABC implementation is acknowledged to be incompletely tuned. There is no strong comparison with surrogate-based, domain-adaptation, low-budget SBI, or recent multifidelity SBI alternatives, even where these are discussed as concurrent work.

A-MF-TSNPE is knowingly statistically biased: actively selected samples are mixed into training without proposal correction. The appendix explicitly acknowledges that its density estimate can diverge from the true posterior and supports the 20% mixture only heuristically. This undermines its interpretation as Bayesian posterior estimation and the strongest simulation-efficiency claim.

Several reporting inconsistencies substantially weaken reproducibility. For example, the L5PC evaluation size is variously reported as 1,000 versus 100 observations; the spiking-network evaluation as 10,000 versus 262,008 observations; and the neuron stimulus as a noisy 0.3 nA current versus a 0.55 mV step. These discrepancies affect central experiments rather than cosmetic details.

The headline claim of up to two orders of magnitude fewer high-fidelity simulations overstates the end-to-end benefit. The supplied cost analysis shows roughly a 4–5x total-cost reduction for L5PC and 10x for the spiking network, while the active method incurs considerable ensemble-training cost.

The spiking-network evidence is relatively weak for a flagship real-world result: it uses only two firing-rate summaries for a 24-dimensional posterior, provides no calibration or ground-truth posterior assessment, and the reported cost-matched NLTP values in Table 5 are not clearly superior to NPE under the paper's lower-is-better definition.

The analysis of when transfer helps is exploratory and narrow. Mutual information is estimated with MINE, representational similarity is represented by one coordinate reversal, and no uncertainty or robustness analysis is given for the claimed predictors of transfer success.

Code and data are promised only upon publication rather than supplied with the submission, limiting verification of the numerous low-budget experiments and implementation-sensitive sequential procedures.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: reducing the number of expensive simulations needed for neural posterior estimation.
The evaluation spans four controlled benchmarks and two comparatively realistic neuroscience simulators, including different observation and parameter dimensions.

The experiments generally show that low-fidelity pretraining improves over randomly initialized NPE at small high-fidelity budgets, and the paper reports wall-clock costs, posterior predictive checks, and some calibration results.
The controlled perturbation study is a useful attempt to characterize when transfer helps, highlighting both shared information and representational alignment.
The manuscript is generally understandable and documents the simulator definitions and normalizing-flow hyperparameters in substantial detail.
weaknesses: The principal method is essentially direct fine-tuning of a standard neural posterior estimator pretrained on low-fidelity simulations. This is intuitive but technically modest, with no new objective, correction mechanism, or theoretical result specific to multifidelity inference; the convergence proof only restates the standard population-risk argument for NPE.

A-MF-TSNPE is not a sound posterior estimator as presented. Acquisition-selected parameters bias the training distribution, yet the method applies no proposal correction. The authors explicitly acknowledge that the estimate can diverge from the true posterior and merely assume that using 20% active samples makes the benefit outweigh the bias. This undermines posterior and calibration claims for a highlighted variant.

The experimental comparisons are insufficient for the broad state-of-the-art claims. Most results compare only against NPE/TSNPE and a reportedly under-tuned MF-ABC implementation. Concurrent multifidelity SBI, active SBI, surrogate-based, and other data-efficient SBI methods are discussed but not evaluated.

Several claimed efficiency comparisons conflate different inference settings: amortized NPE is compared with observation-specific sequential methods, while ensemble training and acquisition overhead differ substantially. Claims of orders-of-magnitude savings are therefore not consistently established under matched objectives and total computational budgets.

The neuroscience studies use synthetic observations from the high-fidelity simulators rather than empirical recordings. They demonstrate simulator recovery but provide limited evidence that the method works under real data/model mismatch, making the language about real-world inference overly strong.

The paper provides weak safeguards against negative transfer. The controlled study only examines one OU construction, and there is no reliable diagnostic, selection rule, or compute-aware criterion for deciding whether and how much to pretrain on a candidate low-fidelity model.

Reproducibility is incomplete because code and data are only promised after publication. There are also reporting inconsistencies, including 10 versus 30 benchmark observations and 10,000 versus 262,008 spiking-network evaluation observations, while the sequential pseudocode is unclear about whether simulations from earlier rounds are retained.

At very small budgets, the stated 10% validation split can contain only about five simulations, making early stopping unstable; sensitivity to data splits and fine-tuning hyperparameters is not adequately studied. Overall, the empirical promise does not compensate for the limited novelty, biased active variant, and incomplete comparisons required for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_iclr2026_yao_medium_20260919T2254Z/scratch/b7d89d65661c474f9542043d2d3dc515/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses an important practical limitation of simulation-based inference: the high cost of accurate simulators. Its transfer-learning formulation is simple, broadly applicable, and compatible with both amortized and sequential neural posterior estimation.
The evaluation is unusually broad, covering four controlled benchmarks and two scientifically meaningful neuroscience simulators, including a challenging 24-parameter spiking-network problem.

Results consistently favor multifidelity initialization in low high-fidelity-budget regimes. The cost analysis also demonstrates meaningful end-to-end savings—approximately 4–10× for closely comparable accuracy on the expensive applications—with larger reductions in the number of high-fidelity simulations in selected settings.

The paper goes beyond aggregate accuracy curves by including multiple metrics, simulation-based calibration, posterior-predictive checks, sensitivity to low-fidelity dataset size, and experiments with mismatched parameter dimensions.

The controlled perturbation study provides useful empirical insight into when transfer succeeds, distinguishing mutual information from representational alignment. The presentation is clear, and the appendices provide substantial implementation and simulator detail.
weaknesses: The central algorithmic novelty is modest: MF-NPE is essentially ordinary fine-tuning of a neural posterior estimator pretrained on low-fidelity data. The paper therefore depends heavily on empirical strength rather than a new inference principle or theoretical guarantee.

Baseline coverage is incomplete. MF-ABC is the only multifidelity competitor and receives an acknowledged limited hyperparameter search; recent multifidelity, response-distillation, surrogate-based, and active-learning SBI approaches discussed in related work are not compared experimentally.

A-MF-TSNPE adds acquisition-selected parameters to the standard posterior-estimation objective without proposal correction. The appendix explicitly acknowledges potential bias and justifies it by using a minority of active samples, but this is not a principled guarantee. Moreover, the active variant improves only the OU task consistently while adding substantial ensemble-training cost.

The strongest savings claims partly compare methods at unequal accuracy. For example, the cost table shows A-MF-TSNPE using 50 rather than 10,000 L5PC simulations, but its NLTP is appreciably worse; the more closely matched MF-NPE comparison supports a smaller, though still valuable, reduction.

Results on the realistic tasks rely mainly on NLTP/NRMSE or a two-dimensional firing-rate plausibility criterion because the true posterior is unavailable. Calibration is shown only for the L5PC task, leaving uncertainty quality on the 24-parameter spiking-network task insufficiently validated.

Important experimental details are inconsistent across sections: the L5PC stimulus is reported as a noisy 0.3 nA current in the main text but as a 0.55 mV step in the appendix, and evaluation-set sizes differ between the main text, captions, and training-details appendix. Code and data are promised only after publication. These issues reduce current reproducibility.

The method presumes that experts can supply a cheap, sufficiently aligned low-fidelity simulator. The controlled study confirms that misaligned representations can erase the benefit, but the paper offers no practical diagnostic or safeguard against negative transfer before expensive high-fidelity data are collected.
